title: Seed reserve notes from the Lorn Basin transect
public_context: Field ecologists often compare the seeds recovered from soil cores with the seedlings that appear later in a season. A core is a small sample of a larger patch, and the number of intact seeds in it need not predict emergence at that exact spot. Floods, buried layers, and seasonal dormancy can all complicate comparisons across visits.
source_title: Lorn Basin seed reserve field memorandum
source_text:
The Lorn Basin team sampled the north and south benches after the spring flood of 14 April. At each bench, staff took twelve soil cores along a fixed 30-metre tape, keeping the upper five centimetres separate from the five-to-ten-centimetre layer. The paired depths mattered because the low bench had received a thin silt deposit, while the higher bench showed no visible new layer. A marked stake was moved after the flood, so the team relocated its line from two surviving stone markers rather than from the old stake.

In the laboratory, technicians washed each layer through a two-millimetre screen and counted intact seeds by species. Recoverable seed density in the north bench's upper layer was nearly twice its autumn count, while the deeper layer changed little. The south bench showed no comparable increase. The field notes attribute the north rise to seed-bearing silt carried from an upstream slope, but they call that explanation provisional because no source-slope sample was taken.

A separate emergence tray test used subsamples kept separate by bench and by sampled depth. The trays stayed under the same light cycle for six weeks, with water added by mass rather than by visual judgment. Several sedge seeds from the deeper north layer germinated only after the final cool-to-warm transition. The team therefore recorded recovered seeds and emerged seedlings as different measures; it did not convert the tray count into a forecast for the whole basin.

The team did not interpret a high count in a single core as proof that seedlings would emerge there. Cores at the north line varied widely, and one unusually dense upper-layer core lay beside a shallow runnel. The report kept that core in the summary instead of deleting it, while flagging the runnel as a possible local deposit. No seed was classified as dormant solely because its coat looked intact; staff used the tray response and a cut test on a small remainder.

On the second visit, volunteers found new seedlings mainly along the bench edge, not evenly across the taped line. Their map was made after a short rain and was not paired with fresh cores, so it cannot show whether those seedlings came from the measured reserve or arrived later. The memorandum recommends repeating the depth-separated cores before the next flood and keeping the old and new seedling maps side by side. It gives no estimate of how much of the north increase will persist through summer drying.
authoring_note: The main structure links a flood-related change in a stratified seed reserve to later but unpaired emergence observations, with a named causal explanation left provisional.

supported_claims.claim: The team sampled both benches after the April spring flood and separated two soil depths.
evidence: The Lorn Basin team sampled the north and south benches after the spring flood of 14 April. At each bench, staff took twelve soil cores along a fixed 30-metre tape, keeping the upper five centimetres separate from the five-to-ten-centimetre layer.

supported_claims.claim: The north upper layer had nearly twice its autumn recoverable seed density, while its deeper layer changed little.
evidence: Recoverable seed density in the north bench's upper layer was nearly twice its autumn count, while the deeper layer changed little.

supported_claims.claim: The report provisionally attributes the north rise to seed-bearing silt but lacks an upstream source-slope sample.
evidence: The field notes attribute the north rise to seed-bearing silt carried from an upstream slope, but they call that explanation provisional because no source-slope sample was taken.

supported_claims.claim: The emergence tray test kept subsamples separate by bench and sampled depth; several deeper north sedge seeds germinated only after the final cool-to-warm transition.
evidence: A separate emergence tray test used subsamples kept separate by bench and by sampled depth.
Several sedge seeds from the deeper north layer germinated only after the final cool-to-warm transition.

supported_claims.claim: A dense core near a runnel was retained and flagged as a possible local deposit.
evidence: The report kept that core in the summary instead of deleting it, while flagging the runnel as a possible local deposit.

supported_claims.claim: The later seedling map was not paired with fresh cores and cannot identify the measured reserve as the seedlings' source.
evidence: Their map was made after a short rain and was not paired with fresh cores, so it cannot show whether those seedlings came from the measured reserve or arrived later.

explicit_negatives.claim: The team did not treat a high count in one core as proof of local emergence.
evidence: The team did not interpret a high count in a single core as proof that seedlings would emerge there.

explicit_negatives.claim: An intact-looking seed coat alone was not used to classify a seed as dormant.
evidence: No seed was classified as dormant solely because its coat looked intact; staff used the tray response and a cut test on a small remainder.

licensed_inferences.claim: The north upper-layer increase could reflect deposition that was spatially uneven, but the report does not establish its source or basin-wide persistence.
licensed_inferences.rationale: The measured increase, provisional upstream-silt account, and unusually dense runnel-side core jointly fit patchy deposition; the missing source sample and single local core prevent stronger attribution.

licensed_inferences.claim: The later edge seedlings cannot be used as a direct validation of the earlier core-based reserve measurements.
licensed_inferences.rationale: The tray response was a separate controlled measure, while the later field map had no paired cores and left later arrival possible.

unspecified_probes.neutral_question: Were the soil cores dried before washing?
unspecified_probes.presupposition_question: Were all soil cores dried overnight in the north shed before washing?
unspecified_probes.candidate_claim: All cores were dried overnight in the north shed before washing.
unspecified_probes.boundary_note: The memorandum describes washing and counting but gives no drying location or duration; neither the candidate nor its negation is established.

unspecified_probes.neutral_question: What color labels were attached to the sample containers?
unspecified_probes.presupposition_question: Did staff use blue labels on every north-bench sample container?
unspecified_probes.candidate_claim: Every north-bench sample container had a blue label.
unspecified_probes.boundary_note: No label color is reported, and sample separation by depth does not imply a particular label scheme.

unspecified_probes.neutral_question: What was the north upper-layer seed density after summer drying?
unspecified_probes.presupposition_question: Did the north upper-layer reserve remain above its autumn count after summer drying?
unspecified_probes.candidate_claim: The north upper-layer reserve remained above its autumn count after summer drying.
unspecified_probes.boundary_note: The report supplies no persistence estimate, but does not state that the reserve fell below its autumn count or that it remained elevated.

consistency_questions.question: How should the provisional silt explanation be weighed against the unusually dense runnel-side core?
consistency_questions.reference_answer: The local concentration and provisional transport account are compatible with uneven deposition, but the unsampled source slope and one flagged core leave both source and scale uncertain.

consistency_questions.question: What can the tray germination and later field map jointly establish about the measured reserve?
consistency_questions.reference_answer: The tray shows that some recovered seeds could germinate after a temperature transition, while the unpaired field map cannot establish that later seedlings came from those measured seeds or validate emergence at a particular core.
